messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Warning in tgamma
parts:
For 1, it's best to reparameterize if increasing adapt_delta to 0.99 or
something like that doesn't remove the divergent transitions. It
means the sampler's getting into a region where it can't reliably
follow the Hamiltonian.

Did you run multiple chains?

2. The code's running int numerical problems evaluating the
gamma function (like factorial, it can't take very large inputs
without overflowing---better to work on the log scale where
possible and use lgamma instead of tgamma in the Stan code).
For example, you compute gamma_nu as tgamma(nu/2) and then
take the log of it -- just use lgamma(nu / 2) and work on
the log scale all along here.

There are a lot of problems with the way the program is
coded. You usually want to use Cholesky factors for parameters
and use matrix division rather than inversion.

3. Parallelizing multiple chains with the number of cores
you have should be faster unless you're running out of memory.

As general advice, I'd suggest fitting simpler models here
to start and woking up to this complex mixture model after
fitting the components.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Warning in tgamma
parts:
> On Jan 30, 2017, at 11:39 AM, Elaheh Torkashvand <torkas...@gmail.com> wrote:
> ...use matrix division rather than inversion.

>
>
> Are you referring to how Sigma_model_inverse is modelled? I already changed the code to remove Sigma_model_inverse by replacing it by (trajectory[n]-mu_model[1]) / Sigma_model. Following your comment I generated Sigma_model using Cholesky factors.

Great. That's right, you want to replace inv(A) * B with A \ B and A * inv(B)
with A / B. Or if it's all part of one big compound operation, implement
that operation with matrix derivatives in C++ (that's not a user operation---it's
a dev thing, but it's what we do in these cases if it's a model we're going
to reuse).

> 3. Parallelizing multiple chains with the number of cores
> you have should be faster unless you're running out of memory.
>
>
> I run my code on WestGrid system (Compute Canada). In terms of memory, the program is doing fine. However, when I use parallel, the speed reduces significantly. Does it make sense to say it takes time for the system to find all cores available and run the program? As you have seen the code there is no bug related to coding of this part.

Running in parallel shouldn't be any slower to sample. Finding
multiple cores should be trivial. It's not something that you
can control from within a Stan program anyway. I have no idea
about R. One issue that can come up in cluster computing is
communication overhead. I think there's a way to tamp down the
output in RStan (soon we'll be able to get rid of it all). With
clusters, the disk and I/O can be super slow and be a bottleneck.

> As general advice, I'd suggest fitting simpler models here
> to start and woking up to this complex mixture model after
> fitting the components.
>
> Thank you for the time you spent answering my questions.

You're welcome. We like to see people get the most out of Stan
when possible. But hard problems require some thought about
coding that's not so obvious from our manuals and docs (we're
working on that).

- Bob
